entities.summary: Maturinus, or Mathurin, was a Gallo-Roman exorcist and missionary venerated as a saint. Born in the late 3rd century CE, Maturinus rose to prominence during the reign of Emperor Diocletian (284-305 CE). He was instrumental in establishing the Christian Church's presence in Gaul (modern-day France) and wrote several treatises on exorcism and spirituality. Maturinus's influence can be seen in the development of monasticism, particularly in the establishment of the monastery at Lérins Island, where he spent his final years. The 4th-century historian Gregory of Tours praised Maturinus as a 'model of piety' and a 'glorious martyr.' Despite the passing of centuries, Maturinus's legacy endures through his writings and the countless miracles attributed to him by devotees.

Figures", "comparative-religion", "doctrine-development", "cultural-diffusion"], "thumbnailUrl": "", "quote": "", "legacySummary": "", "summary": "Saint Maturinus (also Mathurin or Materne; died c. 388 CE, or by some traditions c. 301 CE) was a Christian confessor and saint of the late Roman period — associated with Larchant (Roman Larca/Larcha) in the Gâtinais region of what is now north-central France (Seine-et-Marne, Île-de-France). He is venerated in the Catholic Church and his feast day is celebrated on 1 November in some local traditions and on 9 November in the Roman Martyrology. Maturinus is the patron saint of Larchant and is traditionally credited with the evangelisation of the Gâtinais region, with exorcising the daughter of the Roman emperor Maximianus (a legendary element typical of early Christian hagiography), and with working miracles of healing.

The historical evidence for Maturinus is almost entirely hagiographic: his life is known primarily through the 'Vita Sancti Maturini' composed much later than the events it purports to describe, and the historical details (including the story of Maximianus's daughter) are standard hagiographic topoi. What can be said with more confidence is that Maturinus was venerated in the Gâtinais region from an early period — the medieval pilgrimage church of Saint-Mathurin at Larchant was one of the major pilgrimage centres of the Île-de-France, attracting pilgrims from across the region throughout the medieval period. The 13th-century Gothic church of Saint-Mathurin at Larchant, built to accommodate the pilgrimage cult, was a significant medieval architectural achievement whose imposing tower (now ruined) is still a regional landmark.

Maturinus became associated in popular tradition with madness and mental illness — as the patron who could cure insanity — and this association gave his name to the 'Maisons de Mathurins' (later 'Maisons des fous'), the French institutions for the mentally ill. The 'Mathurins' designation for religious orders who ran charitable institutions reflects the popular association between Saint Mathurin and charitable care of the afflicted. Maturinus, or Mathurin was a Gallo-Roman exorcist and missionary venerated as a saint. He was born in Gaul (modern-day France) and died in 301 CE. As an early Christian, Maturinus played a significant role in spreading Christianity throughout the Roman Empire, particularly among the Celtic tribes of Britain and Ireland.

Maturinus' ministry involved exorcisms, healings, and pastoral care for his flock. He was known for his piety, humility, and unwavering commitment to his faith. His legacy as a saint has endured for centuries, inspiring countless devotionals, artworks, and literary works. In the 7th century CE, Pope Gregory II designated Maturinus as a saint of the Western Church, solidifying his place in Christian canonization.

Despite the passage of time, Maturinus' impact on Christian history remains profound. His missionary work and exorcistic practices continue to influence modern Catholicism, while his example of devotion and humility serves as an inspiration for countless Christians around the world.

One striking statistic illustrating Maturinus' significance is the number of churches and shrines dedicated to his memory across Europe.
